findings.statement: Broadcom’s custom AI accelerators (XPUs) have been adopted by several hyperscale cloud operators. The company has secured design contracts with Google and Meta, and in October 2025 announced a strategic collaboration with OpenAI to deploy OpenAI‑designed AI accelerators; OpenAI’s deployments are being built and rolled out in partnership with Broadcom. Analysts also cite ByteDance (TikTok parent) as a fourth customer receiving AI rack orders.

Broadcom’s roadmap for the next 12‑24 months includes mass‑production of its 3.5D XDSiP‑based XPU platform and the 2 nm custom compute SoC announced in February 2026. The company also plans to roll out next‑generation Ethernet switches such as the 102.4 Tbps Tomahawk 6, the ultra‑low‑latency Tomahawk Ultra (250 ns), and the Jericho 4 fabric designed for clusters exceeding one million XPUs. Additionally, Broadcom co‑leads the Optical Scale‑up Consortium to define open specifications for future AI interconnects.

Broadcom announced an extended partnership with Meta to support Meta's custom MTIA silicon using Broadcom's XPU platform and Ethernet‑based rack‑scale interconnects. The announcement describes this as the first deployment in a multi‑generation roadmap that will span the next several years, indicating upcoming AI accelerator and networking hardware offerings.

AMD reports that the Instinct MI300X delivers up to 1,307.4 TFLOPS of FP16 (and BF16) performance and 2,614.9 TFLOPS of FP8 / 2,614.9 TOPS of INT8 throughput. The Instinct MI350X provides up to 2.05× higher FP6 performance than NVIDIA’s B200 platform, while the Instinct MI355X offers roughly 2× higher FP6 performance versus NVIDIA’s GB200 platform.

AMD announced that within the next 12 months it will ship the Instinct MI455X GPU (part of the MI400 series) and the Instinct MI350P PCIe accelerator, both positioned for the Helios rack‑scale AI solution and supported by ongoing ROCm software enhancements.

AMD offers the Instinct MI300X (launched 2023), MI325X (2024), MI350 series (2025) and MI355X (2025) GPUs as AI‑focused accelerators for data‑center training and inference. The GPUs use CDNA architectures, provide up to 288 GB of HBM3E memory and are marketed as production‑ready platforms for large‑scale generative AI workloads.

AMD: Oracle is building a 27,000‑plus node AI cluster that incorporates AMD Instinct MI355X accelerators, 5th‑Gen EPYC "Turin" CPUs and AMD Pensando Pollara 400 SmartNICs, representing a large‑scale deployment of AMD GPUs in a U.S. cloud service environment.

AMD’s 2025 annual report states that record Instinct GPU revenue, driven by the MI350 series, contributed to Data Center net revenue of $16.6 billion—a 32 % year‑over‑year increase—highlighting the financial impact of its AI accelerator business.

AMD announced the ROCm 7 software stack, which provides more than three‑times higher training and inference performance compared with the prior generation, with the release scheduled for 2025 (within the next 12 months).

Intel Corp: Intel markets several AI‑specific hardware products for data‑center AI workloads, including the Intel® Gaudi® AI accelerators (Gaudi 2 and the announced Gaudi 3), the Intel® Data Center GPU Flex Series, and AI‑enabled Intel® Xeon® processors.

Intel Corp: Major cloud providers have adopted Intel AI hardware: IBM Cloud offers Intel Gaudi 3 accelerators as a service, and Amazon EC2 instances in the United States and Europe are provisioned with Intel Xeon CPUs and Intel Gaudi 2 accelerators for AI workloads.

Intel Corp: Intel announced a new data‑center GPU, code‑named “Crescent Island,” optimized for AI inference, with a 160 GB LPDDR5X memory configuration and sampling expected in the second half of 2026.

Intel Corp: Intel markets a portfolio of AI‑specific hardware for data‑center AI workloads, including the Data Center GPU Flex Series (Flex 170), the Data Center GPU Max Series, Intel® Gaudi® AI Accelerators (Gaudi 2 and Gaudi 3), integrated AI engines built into Xeon processors, and Intel® FPGAs for AI.

Intel Corp: Intel’s Gaudi 3 AI accelerator delivers up to 40% faster time‑to‑train than an equivalent‑size Nvidia H100 GPU cluster (8,192 accelerators) and 15% higher training throughput for a 64‑accelerator cluster on Llama2‑70B; inference performance is up to 2× faster on Llama‑70B models. Independent Signal65 testing shows Gaudi 3 achieving 43%‑97% more tokens per second than Nvidia H100/H200 across batch sizes, and 1.8× better performance‑per‑dollar on LLaMA 3 8B inference.

Intel Corp: Major cloud providers have adopted Intel AI hardware in their US and European data centers: IBM Cloud offers Intel Gaudi 3 as a service (announced in the Q3 2024 earnings call and detailed in a white paper), Microsoft Azure integrates Intel AI optimizations on its CPU instances and supports Intel extensions for Scikit‑learn, PyTorch and OpenVINO, and Google Cloud provides C4 and N4 VM instances powered by Intel Xeon 6 processors for AI workloads. No specific volume numbers are disclosed.

Intel Corp: Intel markets the Gaudi2 AI accelerator (acquired from Habana) and Intel Xeon processors as core components for data‑center AI workloads, positioning them for use in large AI supercomputers and cloud AI services.
Intel Corp: In April 2026 Intel disclosed a deeper collaboration with Google to advance AI infrastructure, highlighting joint efforts to build open, scalable AI platforms for cloud environments.

Broadcom’s Tomahawk Ultra Ethernet switch is advertised with a 250 ns end‑to‑end latency for AI workloads. The Jericho4 AI network router, fabricated on a 3 nm process, offers 3.2 Tbps “HyperPort” bandwidth per port, supports up to 36,000 HyperPorts, and uses 200 G PAM4 SerDes, delivering low‑power, high‑throughput interconnect for large AI clusters.

Broadcom currently offers its custom XPU family of AI accelerators, marketed as “custom XPUs,” which are integrated into AI‑optimized racks for both training and inference workloads in data centers. The company also supplies high‑throughput Ethernet switching silicon, notably the Tomahawk 6 switch delivering 102 Tbps of bandwidth, and associated AI networking components that form the interconnect fabric for hyperscale AI clusters. These products are positioned for cloud service providers and AI developers building large‑scale AI infrastructure.
Intel Corp: For fiscal year 2025, Intel’s DCAI segment generated $16.92 billion, representing roughly 32 % of the company’s consolidated revenue.
Intel Corp: In 2023, Intel’s DCAI business produced $19.4 billion in revenue, accounting for about 78 % of its total revenue that year.

Broadcom reported AI semiconductor revenue of $16.7 billion in Q3 FY2026, representing 56% of total revenue ($29.59 billion). In Q1 FY2026 the company posted $8.4 billion of AI revenue, roughly 43% of total quarterly revenue ($19.31 billion). These disclosures indicate that AI computing products constitute a majority share of Broadcom's overall revenue in recent periods.
NVIDIA's AI computing portfolio includes accelerated compute GPUs, DGX data‑center systems, networking, AI software, and cloud access.
Internal guidance emphasizes comparing whole‑system design, integration, deployment requirements, and service/support rather than focusing solely on processor specifications.
Broadcom's custom‑accelerator offerings may be tied to specific customers, clouds, or workloads and should not be assumed broadly purchasable.
Potential buyer roles for cloud service providers include infrastructure leadership, data‑center engineering, procurement, capacity planning, cloud product management, and service operations.
